stem:
A 68-year-old man with a prior myocardial infarction presents with progressive dyspnea and orthopnea. Examination shows elevated jugular venous pressure and bilateral crackles. Echocardiography reveals a dilated left ventricle with a markedly depressed ejection fraction. Despite an elevated end-diastolic volume, his forward stroke volume remains low.

Which of the following best explains why the Frank–Starling mechanism fails to restore adequate output in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased preload has abolished venous return to the heart
options.misconception: High filling is being treated as loss of venous return.
options.explanation: Venous return and preload are elevated; the problem is that the damaged myocardium cannot convert that stretch into an adequate stroke volume.

options.label: B
options.text: Reduced contractility flattens the stretch–force relationship
options.misconception: None; a weak ventricle sits on a depressed Frank–Starling curve.
options.explanation: Frank–Starling links greater stretch to stronger contraction only within limits and for a given inotropic state; after infarction, reduced contractility flattens that curve so elevated end-diastolic volume no longer yields adequate stroke volume.

options.label: C
options.text: Decreased afterload prevents the ventricle from ejecting
options.misconception: Low afterload is being blamed for low output.
options.explanation: Lower afterload would favor ejection; in systolic failure the limiting factor is reduced contractility, often with elevated afterload from vasoconstriction.

options.label: D
options.text: Heart rate alone determines stroke volume in dilated ventricles
options.misconception: Rate is being substituted for the length–tension mechanism.
options.explanation: Heart rate multiplies stroke volume to give cardiac output; it does not replace preload–contractility coupling as the per-beat mechanism.

options.label: E
options.text: Increased ventricular compliance cancels any effect of stretch
options.misconception: A compliance change is being treated as the reason stretch fails.
options.explanation: Compliance affects how filling pressure maps to volume; the failed output here reflects depressed contractility on the Frank–Starling curve, not cancelled stretch from compliance alone.

context: Learning objective: recognize when Frank–Starling cannot compensate. In systolic heart failure, reduced contractility depresses the stretch–force curve so elevated preload no longer restores stroke volume.
